Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette: John, a 46-year-old African American park ranger married to his high school sweetheart, has struggled since returning from combat. The memories of the traumatic event continue to haunt him, shaping his current experience and behavior. During one particularly vivid memory, John recalls the intense smell of smoke and burning rubber that filled the air as helicopters buzzed overhead, carrying wounded soldiers. This sensory experience is deeply embedded in his memory, making the sound of any aircraft or helicopter a powerful trigger. Whenever he hears such sounds now, whether it's during his daily patrols or when passing by an airport, John feels an immediate surge of discomfort and begins to feel detached from reality. These triggers heighten his sense of threat, leaving him on high alert for unexpected or loud noises and constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of danger. This hypervigilance has become a constant in his life, not just at work but also during family gatherings at home. John’s wife has noticed that he seems distant and more anxious than before the deployment. He is always watching others closely for any sign they might harm him, even in familiar settings like the park where he works or in their own home. This constant threat monitoring exacerbates his feelings of being permanently damaged by the traumatic event. John believes he will never forgive himself for not doing enough to prevent the tragic outcomes he witnessed, and this guilt further fuels his hypervigilance. The vividness and clarity of his memories contribute significantly to his negative appraisals. When John recalls the event, the olfactory cues and visual details feel more real and immediate than any other memory from his life. These powerful recollections reinforce his belief that he has been irrevocably changed for the worse. His constant scanning for danger only intensifies these memories, making them even more vivid and triggering further negative appraisals. This cycle has become self-reinforcing; John’s hypervigilance leads to a heightened sense of threat, which in turn triggers his traumatic memories and fuels his negative appraisals. This loop of discomfort and distress makes it difficult for him to engage fully with life. The weight of these experiences has strained his relationships, particularly with his wife who feels increasingly isolated as John withdraws into himself. What finally brought John to seek help was a recent incident where the sound of an airplane passing over the park triggered a severe reaction. He felt so disconnected and overwhelmed that he had to leave work early, and this marked a turning point for him. Despite his fears about being vulnerable again, John is hopeful that with support, he can break free from these overwhelming memories and begin to reclaim some sense of normalcy in his life. John’s primary fear is the idea that he will never fully recover and that his family and career will continue to suffer as a result of his inability to cope. He hopes for understanding and support, believing that with help, he can start to navigate these challenges more effectively.
